title: Fair Isle fingerless mitts
subtitle: Two-colour peerie bands in the round, with afterthought thumb.
excerpt: Fingerless mitts with traditional Fair Isle peerie bands (small two-colour geometric repeats), worked in the round in DK wool. Afterthought thumb. Sized for hand circumferences of 18, 20, and 22 cm.
sourceNotes: Traditional Fair Isle peerie patterns are folk designs from Shetland, UK, recorded in the Shetland Museum and Archive collection and in Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938), §Colourwork. The specific band arrangement here is an original combination of public-domain motifs.

knitting.gaugeText: 24 sts × 28 rounds = 10 × 10 cm in two-colour stranded stocking stitch on 3.75 mm needles, blocked.
knitting.finishedSizeText: Hand circumference 18 (20, 22) cm with 1 to 2 cm negative ease.

glossaryTerms.definition: A small Fair Isle motif, typically 3 to 5 rounds tall, used as a border or fill between larger pattern blocks. The word peerie is Shetland dialect for small. Peerie bands are worked in two colours with no float longer than 5 stitches.

A technique where two or more yarn colours are carried across each round, with the unused colour floating as a strand on the wrong side. Both colours are picked up and set down as needed to form the pattern.

A thumb opening made by working the thumb stitches in waste yarn during the hand, then returning to them after the hand is complete. The waste yarn is removed to reveal live stitches which are picked up and worked as the thumb.
A method for knitting small circumferences in the round on one long circular needle. The cable is pulled into a loop at the midpoint so each half of the stitches sits on its own needle tip.

content.text: 24 stitches and 28 rounds to 10 cm in two-colour stranded stocking stitch on 3.75 mm needles, blocked. The colourwork gauge is tighter than single-colour gauge at the same needle size. Swatch in two colours and compare before casting on.

items.name: Round 1
items.qty: CC1 MC3, repeat (CC on stitch 1 of every 4)

content.text: Before you cast on, circle your size. Every stitch count reads S (M, L) for hand circumferences 18 (20, 22) cm.

Using MC and the long-tail cast-on, cast on 40 (44, 48) stitches (2 more per size than single-colour mitts to compensate for tighter colourwork gauge). Join to work in the round. Work 2×2 rib in MC for 20 (22, 24) rounds.

Work Band A (3 rounds). Then work 8 (10, 10) rounds in MC stocking stitch. Work Band B (5 rounds). At the start of the first Band B round, place the thumb: knit 8 (9, 10) stitches with waste yarn, slip back and re-knit with MC, then continue the Band B round. Work 8 (10, 10) rounds in MC stocking stitch. Work Band A (3 rounds). Work 4 rounds of 2×2 rib in MC. Bind off in rib.

Remove waste yarn and pick up 8 (9, 10) stitches above and below the gap. Total: 16 (18, 20) thumb stitches. Work 10 (12, 12) rounds in MC stocking stitch. Decrease round: (k1, k2tog) across. Draw yarn through to close.
Float too long in Band B: the cross-and-dot repeat has one section of 5 MC stitches. Trap the CC float by laying it across the back of these 5 stitches and catching it under one of them at mid-span.

Band misaligned at the thumb gap: the thumb waste yarn was worked mid-band, which disrupts the repeat at that point. Accept the small disruption, or place the thumb gap so it lands at a band boundary rather than mid-band.
Weave all tails in on the wrong side. Wet-block and pin the bands square before drying.
Hand wash in cool water with a wool-safe detergent. Re-block flat after washing.
From here, the natural next step is a full Fair Isle yoke sweater, where the same peerie bands appear as accent stripes between the main colourwork panels.
